ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: answers on the map
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: When an answer says people do something, they do it: a feast is eaten, a fire lit, a grave visited, a work party sent out, a watch kept at the gate, medicine carried out to the rider.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Keep a few cooked meals and a few free hands: the answers you choose may need both.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description:
With "Answers play out on the map" on (the Events and world page of the settings, on by default), an answer to a dilemma, a Rimfolk event, a story or a world event that describes something people do happens on the map. A message says when it starts and where, This week lists it under "Gatherings and plans" while it waits and while it goes on, and the dilemmas page says how it went. The good moods the answer gives the people it names come to them once they have taken part; if it never comes about, everyone gets them anyway, as answers always did. When the answer is given you only hear when it's planned; the answer's own words for what happened ("They danced until the fire was embers...") come once it's over. An answer that says no, tells of something far away, or of something that happened before the letter came, sets nothing going and is told at once.
The same goes beyond answers. When a personal story reaches a stage that says someone does something (sits by a grave, sits up by the fire telling the road, hands over a gift they made, tells a secret to the gathered colony, keeps watch by a child's bed), they do it, and so do a few moments with visitors: a guest shown round, a lesson in the yard, an evening of songs, a bowl carried out to a traveler. In all, 431 answers of 134 dilemmas and 125 events, stories and world events play out (up from 421 of 133 dilemmas before gifts went by hand and lanterns, fires and pyres were kept on the map), with 20 stages of 17 personal stories (up from 15 of 13) and 7 moments with visitors.

li.heading: What can happen

table.li: Feast | Everyone who comes eats a cooked meal from the stores, the finest first they may eat | Ate, or stayed a while
Gathering, bonfire, toast | The colony gathers round the table, a fire, a stranger or a grave, and a toast is drunk | Stayed a while

Words (a lesson, a story, a letter read out) | The speaker stands at the head of the table; the listeners take the chairs round it, facing them, and the rest stand close by (with no table near, a ring round the speaker). A visiting scholar teaching comes to the table for it | Stayed a while

Visit, lesson | One goes to sit with someone, by a grave, at the camp's fire, the water, the field's edge or the gate (the open air, if the answer allows it, when there's no water or field near), or works at a teacher's side | Half of it
Work party | A few clean, haul, mend, build, carry the dead, clear snow, sow, shear and milk, or bring in the harvest together | A job done, or a quarter of it at work
Walk together | They gather, walk out to a grave, the gate, the fields, the water or far out, stand a while and walk back | Half the stay at the far end

Vigil | They keep watch at a grave, the gate, the fields or someone's bedside, into the night; a night watch walks the colony's edge from one look-out to the next until dawn | A third of it, at most two hours
Search | They fan out over the land, each their own way, and look over a few places; the find is given at the end | Half their places
Errand | Someone carries real things from the stores out to a visitor or to the rider at the gate | Handed over
Hunt | The hunters go after the game the answer marked | The game brought down

Handed over | The one a thing is from carries it over to the one it's for and sets it down at their feet; a thing a visitor made is collected from beside them and taken in to the table; a stash is carried out to the yard and burned | Handed over
Rounds | One goes round to each of up to 8 colonists in turn, the nearest first, a few minutes with each: a doctor looking everyone over, a pot of soup for those working outside | Half of them seen
The dead carried out | A few carry the raiders' bodies out one at a time, with the game's own hauling, to a pyre beyond the gate or to the tree line (at most 12) | A body carried out

li.after: What an answer teaches the colony (a visiting scholar's lesson, say) is learned by those who take part, when it's over, and the closing message says who learned what and how much. If it never comes about, everyone it was for learns it anyway, as with the moods.

li.heading: Work parties
li.text:
A work party uses the game's own work: the same jobs a colonist would take on their own, on what the colony really has to do. Filth in the home area, things lying about, damaged buildings, blueprints and frames waiting for materials, the dead, snow where the colony clears it, growing zones to sow, animals ready for shearing or milking, ripe crops and plants marked for harvest. One more kind of work isn't the game's own: bringing the herd home, where each of them goes out to an animal of the herd grazing in the open, puts a rope on it the game's way and walks it into its pen or the barn. Nothing is made up for them to do: with no such work, the party waits, and if there is still none it falls through. Each goes from one job to the next, nearest to where the answer says first (the dining room after a feast), until the time is up or the work runs out.
Only work they are able for: nobody is set to work they're incapable of, and beliefs count. Nobody whose ideoligion is against felling trees is sent to cut them, and nobody whose ideoligion keeps them indoors is sent out to the fields.

li.heading: Walks, vigils and searches
li.text:
A walk together gathers at a gather spot or in the open near the middle of the colony, waits a little for everyone (not long for stragglers), walks out at an easy pace, stands a while at the far end, and walks back. A funeral procession, a walk to the graves to say the names, seeing someone off at the gate, a walk out to look at something.
A vigil is kept by a few, standing in a ring round the grave, the gate or the bed, quietly, from the evening into the night. A low glow shows at the grave or the bed after dark. Each keeps it until it is over, or until hunger or tiredness sends them off: a vigil is not kept at the cost of collapsing.
Searchers each take their own arc of the land round the colony (or round the fields, or along the water), stop at a few places and look about. When they are done, whatever the answer promised (berries, mushrooms, herbs, a few things of the colony's own era) is set down at the feet of the one who found it. If the search never happens or breaks off, the find turns up anyway, where traders leave their goods.

li.heading: Errands and hunts
li.text:
An errand takes from the stores exactly what the answer's taking always took: the same things, the same amount, the quartermaster's saving where there was one. The carrier picks up as much as they can carry and walks it out to the visitor (into their pack) or to the gate, where one of the people it's for waits to take it (see "goods carried by hand"); they fetch the rest from the stores themselves. With nobody to send, the rider or the cart at the gate is only told of, and the rest goes on the cart. Food carried out to others leaves human and insect meat for last. If the errand never happens, or the setting is off, the things leave the stores at once, as before. The answer is greyed out without enough, just as it was.
A hunt marks safe game (never a predator, an insect, anything likely to turn on its hunters, anything bigger than a muffalo or an elk, anyone's animal, an animal bonded to someone, or one the colony's ideoligion venerates) and sends the colony's hunters after it with the game's own hunting: only those with a hunting weapon, no brawlers, and nobody whose beliefs hold violence abhorrent or killing animals wrong. If the game gets away, it stays marked.

li.heading: Things an answer makes real
li.text:
Some answers say a thing now exists, and where it can, it does. A carving made as an apology, a replacement for a broken keepsake, or the gift that settles an old debt is a real small sculpture, signed by the one who made it, its quality from their skill, packed for moving; the one who made it carries it over and sets it down at the feet of the one it's for, and the good moods the answer gives the two wait until it's handed over. An old crafter passing on their craft hands the student their old knife the same way. A scribe's bound copy of the colony's story is a real book with the scribe's name on it, which the one who asked for it collects and takes in to the table. A coffin made ready is a wooden sarcophagus standing in a corner of its owner's room (against a wall, clear of the bed and the door), assigned to them as their grave, if the colony could build one. Two colonists who trade rooms really trade beds, when each sleeps alone and the room given up is the warmer. A hat bought on the side is a real hat, if the colony's era has one. When a guest, a hired hand or the camp's people cut wood, real trees come down near where they are (ordinary timber outside the home area and the colony's zones, never anything sown or marked, at most six), and the logs lie by the stumps; with no tree to be had, or anyone at home whose faith is against felling, the logs are set down where the work was done. The children's trees are real saplings of the kind that grows wild here, at the edge of the fields, each with a stone of the local rock beside it. A room staked out for someone is placed as building plans, the way the room planner places one, at the spot it would suggest and with your planner settings. And a stash searched for in someone's own room is really burned: the addictive drugs they carry and those in a bedroom nobody else sleeps in, with ash in the yard to show it.
Nothing is made that the colony couldn't have: no thing from beyond its era or from a DLC or mod it doesn't have, and when it can't be done the answer's words stand on their own.

li.heading: When it waits, and when it stops

points.li: Each has its hours (an evening feast waits for the evening, a vigil for dusk) and waits a few hours more for its moment: no danger, and its people free.
Nobody is called from eating, sleeping, a sickbed, someone else's care or anything the player ordered.
Any danger ends it at once; so does drafting, being downed, a mental break, or hunger and tiredness for whoever feels them.
Work parties, walks, vigils, searches, errands and hunts never hold anyone in a gathering of their own: the game's parties, rituals and weddings can always take them.
At most eight people go on one; at most two of them are under way at once; none runs more than four hours, or eight for a vigil.
It all saves with the game, and picks up again after a load.

li.heading: What you hear
li.text: Whoever leads it says something as they set off, and now and then someone on it says a line, in their own voice and as the speech setting shows it. Afterwards one or two of those who took part write about it in their journals; if it never came about, whoever was waiting for it may write that too.

li.heading: Kept for a night, or a few
li.text:
Some answers keep something on the map for a while, and take it away again. On lantern night, real torches are set out at dusk along the outside of the colony's walls, a few steps apart and never in a doorway or a zone (one beside the gate, for a single lantern); they burn the wood the answer set aside, nobody carries more out to them, and they're taken in at first light. An old colonist who can't get warm gets a campfire in a free corner of their room, if the room is cold, fed with the wood the answer put by; it's cleared away when that wood is burned, unless you refuel it by hand, and then it's yours to keep.
When the enemy dead are carried out to a pyre beyond the gate, it's lit at dusk: their gear is left in a heap beside it, the bodies burn on a fire laid there, and by morning it's ash. Bodies carried to the tree line are left there, forbidden, so nobody carries them back. A sleepwalker's door is bolted for three nights: only the single door of a bedroom nobody else sleeps in, from ten at night until five, and only once they're in bed; it's let open at once for danger, a fire, a wound, hunger or a sickbed, and drafted colonists pass it as always. And an animal that has taken to following its person keeps at their heels for a day and a half, except when it eats or sleeps; any danger, drafting, or the person leaving the map ends it, and an animal kept in a pen on a rope never follows.
